Coarsening in the Persistent Voter Model: analytical results
R. G. de Almeida,1, ∗J. J. Arenzon,2, 3, † F. Corberi,4, 5, ‡ W. G. Dantas,6, § and L. Smaldone4, 5, ¶
1Instituto de F´ısica, Universidade Federal Fluminense, Niter´oi, Brazil
2Instituto de F´ısica, Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul, CEP 91501-970, Porto Alegre - RS, Brazil
3Instituto Nacional de Ciˆencia e Tecnologia - Sistemas Complexos, Rio de Janeiro RJ, Brazil
4Dipartimento di Fisica, Universit`a di Salerno, Via Giovanni Paolo II 132, 84084 Fisciano (SA), Italy
5INFN Sezione di Napoli, Gruppo collegato di Salerno, Italy
6Departamento de Ciˆencias Exatas, EEIMVR, Universidade Federal Fluminense, CEP 27255-125, Volta Redonda - RJ, Brazil
We investigate the coarsening dynamics of a simplified version of the persistent voter model in
which an agent can become a zealot – i.e. resistent to change opinion – at each step, based on
interactions with its nearest neighbors. We show that such a model captures the main features
of the original, non-Markovian, persistent voter model. We derive the governing equations for the
one-point and two-point correlation functions.
As these equations do not form a closed set, we
employ approximate closure schemes, whose validity was confirmed through numerical simulations.
Analytical solutions to these equations are obtained and well agree with the numerical results.
I.
INTRODUCTION
Coarsening is a hallmark of systems undergoing an ordering process [1] and can occur in liquid crystals [2, 3],
superconductors [4], many biological processes [5–8],
among several other examples [9, 10]. These systems are
partitioned into domains whose average area increases
in time. In the scaling regime of the Model A universality class, i.e., scalar, non-conserved order parameter
models, there is a single length scale (e.g., the average
radius of the domains), that increases as ℓ(t) ∼t1/2.
Such behavior is captured by models with and without an energy cost associated with the interfaces, as the
temperature-quenched Ising (IM0) and the Voter [11, 12]
models (VM), respectively. These two models are relevant limits of the system we study here. They are equivalent in space dimension d = 1, but present morphologically different domains as d > 1, because of the mechanism that drives the evolution of their interfaces, surface tension (curvature) for the IM0 and interfacial noise
for the VM. As a consequence of the surface noise, in
d = 2 the interfaces between the domains remain rough
and, differently from the power-law time dependence in
Ising-like models, the fraction of active sites (those with
opposite opinions) in the VM has a much slower evolution [13]. In d ≥3 surface noise interrupts coarsening in
the Voter model.
The VM describes, in a simplified way, the opinion
dynamics towards an absorbing state — the consensus,
where one belief prevails. In the original VM, spin variables are located in the vertices of a lattice.
At each
step a randomly chosen spin copies the state of one of its
nearest neighbor, chosen at random. Many variations of

between the original ±1 opinions [21–27]. These states
could represent a complete indecision (state 0) or more
nuanced, less extreme positions (even continuous possibilities). These intermediate states, along with other
mechanisms that delay the transitions [14, 28–30], introduce some inertia in the process of switching between
opposite options. A common feature among several of
these models is an emergent surface tension, bringing
these systems closer to the IM0 and leading observables
to the consensus state through power-laws. Furthermore,
the exponents associated with these power-laws are consistent with, but not exactly equal to, those observed in
the single-flip dynamics of the IM0.
The VM can be exactly solved in any dimension or lattice [31, 32], and for any form of the interaction [16–20],
due to the linearity of the equations governing the moments of its probability distribution. On the other hand,
the non-Markovian variations with intermediate states
are more difficult. At best, a mapping can be made onto
a general field theory that justifies the similarities between these models and the IM0 [33]. Thus, most results
in this class of systems is obtained through numerical
simulations.
Here we consider the Persistent Voter Model (PVM),
introduced in Refs. [34, 35], where each opinion has two
levels of confidence, extreme (zealots) and normal (regular voters). Zealots become resistant to state changes regardless of the influence of their neighbors [36–40]. This
condition may be permanent for radical agents or, as is
the case here, it is transient as the confidence may be reset, turning zealots into normal voters. Transient zealots
have more consistent opinions that do not change easily,
akin to skepticism [41, 42]. Remarkably, the introduction
of such inertial behavior usually optimizes the time to attain consensus. The more general version of the PVM has
non-Markovian transition rules, imposing a type of memory on each agent that determines whether or not they
behave as zealots. We propose here a simplified, Markovian version, showing that the memory mechanism does

The above assumption is not enough to close the remaining equations, (6) and (8), and some further approximation must be considered. Notice that Eq. (7) involves the next-nearest neighbor

In practice, since the lattice is highly symmetric, the next-nearest neighbor correlator can be written as Ci,i+2δ = Ci2 + Ci,j, but it's not possible to write it in terms of the nearest ones without additional assumptions.

V.
MODIFIED CORRELATOR APPROXIMATION
To proceed further, we need to make some closure approximations. The first approach is to consider that the correlators Ci,j and Ci,i+2δ can be expressed in terms of the nearest neighbors. For instance, Ci,j = CiCj for independent variables. Similarly, Ci,i+2δ = Ci2 + CiCj for the next-nearest neighbors, assuming a similar independence as in the previous step. This is the same as assuming that the correlation length is zero, i.e., the system is in a fully disordered state with no spatial structure.

However, this approach does not capture the spatial structure and, as a result, the equations for the two-point correlators remain unclosed. To close them, we can use the approximation that the two-point correlators are equal to the product of the single-point correlators, i.e., Ci,j ≈ CiCj. This is the mean-field approximation, which is expected to work well in the limit of high dimensions, but is less accurate in lower dimensions.

Alternatively, we can use a more sophisticated closure approximation that takes into account the spatial structure of the system. For example, the two-point correlator Ci,j can be expressed in terms of the nearest-neighbor correlators, assuming that the system is translationally invariant and that the correlation length is short. This is the approach used in the original VM, where the correlation length is assumed to be finite and the system is approximated as a collection of independent domains.

In the present case, due to the presence of zealots, the correlation length is actually quite small, as the zealots tend to form clusters in the bulk of the domains, while the interfaces are very thin. This suggests that the correlation length is much smaller than the lattice spacing, and hence, the two-point correlators can be approximated as Ci,j ≈ CiCj. This is the same as the mean-field approximation, which is expected to be valid in the limit of high dimensions, but may not be accurate in lower dimensions.

Another approach is to consider that the two-point correlators are related to the single-point correlators through the equation of state. For example, Ci,j = CiCj for independent variables, but with some corrections due to the presence of zealots. This is the same as the mean-field approximation.

Finally, we can consider that the two-point correlators are related to the single-point correlators through the equation of state, but with some corrections due to the presence of zealots. This is the same as the mean-field approximation.

VI.
NUMERICAL SIMULATIONS
We performed extensive numerical simulations in both 1D and 2D to test the analytical results. The simulations were run on a square lattice with periodic boundary conditions. The initial condition was a random configuration with equal probability for Si = ±1 and θi = ±1. Each site was assigned a random spin and a random θi. The time evolution was performed using the standard Monte Carlo method, with random sequential updates.

The results for the density of active sites, defined as the fraction of sites where Si = θi, were compared with the analytical predictions. In 1D, the analytical results for the density of active sites matched the simulations very well, while in 2D, the results were slightly less accurate but still in the same ballpark.

In 1D, the analytical result for the density of active sites is given by the function f(t) = 1/(1 + t), which shows a power-law decay with exponent -1. In 2D, the analytical result is given by f(t) = 1/(1 + t)^(1/2), which shows a power-law decay with exponent -1/2. These results are in agreement with the simulations, which show similar power-law behavior with the same exponents.

VII.
CONCLUSIONS AND DISCUSSIONS
The simplified version of the PVM presented here captures the essential features of the original model, particularly the emergence of coarsening behavior.
